faq.q: How does GPS use time to find you?
faq.a: Each satellite broadcasts the exact time its signal left. Your receiver measures the delay, turns it into a distance, and with distances to at least four satellites it works out your position and corrects its own clock.
asks: Why does GPS need four satellites?

faq.q: What happens if a GPS clock is wrong?
faq.a: Signals travel about 300 metres in a millionth of a second, so even a tiny clock error makes a big position error. That is why GPS satellites carry atomic clocks that ground stations keep checking.
asks: How accurate do GPS clocks need to be?

faq.a: Weaker gravity up at the satellites makes their clocks run fast by about 45 microseconds a day, while their speed slows them by about 7. The net gain of about 38 microseconds a day is corrected, or GPS would drift by about 10 kilometres daily.
An atomic clock keeps time using the steady natural vibrations of atoms such as caesium or rubidium. GPS satellite clocks stay accurate to within a few billionths of a second.
asks: How does an atomic clock work?

faq.q: Why doesn't my phone need an atomic clock?
faq.a: Your phone uses the signal from a fourth satellite to solve for its own clock error along with its position. So the expensive precise clocks only need to be in the satellites.
asks: How does my phone keep accurate time for GPS?

facts: GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds per day relative to clocks on the ground, because of relativity.
The GPS constellation has at least 24 satellites in medium Earth orbit about 20,200 kilometres up.

quiz.say: A GPS satellite's clock is one millionth of a second wrong. Roughly how far off could your position be?
quiz.show: One microsecond clock error gives about…
quiz.why: Light travels about 300 metres in a millionth of a second, so that is the size of the error.

wrong.1: Light travels much further than that in a millionth of a second.
wrong.2: That is far too much; light goes about 300 metres in that time.
